cross_tool_domains.attrition: Low risk — As a single-wave cross-sectional survey there is no longitudinal panel attrition, and item missingness in the regression analyses is minimal (3,182 of 3,204 surveyed households analyzed; 0.7% missing), although initial survey response rates and item missingness on connection-year dates are not reported.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Serious risk — Identification relies on a cross-sectional modified difference-in-differences interaction (village PETT arrival x no prior title) using a single 2004 post-rollout survey without pre-intervention waves to test parallel trends (p. 8; Note 14, p. 12); village rollout timing may be endogenous (p. 4); village-level baseline wealth and infrastructure capacity are unobserved beyond coarse 3-region fixed effects; and regression covariates include post-treatment 2004 household characteristics (workers, home business ownership, rental income) that may be affected by titling.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate — The paper situates PETT in its statutory context (Legislative Decree 25902 of 1991 and 1996 extension to all rural estates, p. 4) and distinguishes village-level PETT rollout from household PETT title, other title, and no-title status, but reconstructs pre-PETT title status ('no prior title') retrospectively from 2004 self-reports under the assumption that 'other titles' were held prior to PETT rather than linking to cadastre/registry records (Note 19, p. 12).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate risk — Both prior-title classification and all water, sanitation, electricity, 5-year connection, and expenditure outcomes are measured via retrospective household self-reports in the 2004 survey without administrative registry verification, utility billing records, or physical inspection of water source protection and quality.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate — Survey items disaggregate specific water supply modes (indoor tap, outdoor tap, fountain, artisan well/spring, river, tanker truck/vendor), sanitation/septic access, recent network connections, and financing sources (Tables 3 and 6), but rely exclusively on self-report and code all fountains and artisan wells/springs as 'improved water sources' without verifying physical protection, water quality, <1 km distance, or >=20 L/day quantity thresholds noted in Note 16.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate risk — No pre-analysis plan or pre-registered protocol exists, and secondary analyses—including the difference-in-differences propensity-score-matching estimates (p. 9) and monthly water payment regressions (p. 11)—are summarized verbally without reporting point estimates or standard errors.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Moderate risk — The 2004 Land Titling Special Project Survey sampled 3,204 rural households stratified by region (coast, highlands, jungle) to represent PETT program and non-program areas (p. 5), but data collection occurred 4–11 years after PETT rollout began, creating potential post-intervention selection via land sales or out-migration, and primary sampling frame details and response rates are not reported in this paper.

domain_ratings.justification: The study estimates a modified difference-in-differences specification (Eq. 1) comparing untitled ('no prior title') and prior-titled households across PETT program and non-program villages using a single 2004 cross-sectional survey. Because no pre-intervention survey waves exist, the modified parallel-trends assumption—that differences between prior-titled and untitled households would have been identical across early- and late-program villages in the absence of PETT—cannot be tested empirically (p. 8; Note 14). The author explicitly acknowledges that village-level timing of PETT rollout might be endogenous (p. 4) and that unobserved village wealth differences could bias the modified DD estimates (p. 8; Note 20). Only three broad regional fixed effects (coast, highlands, jungle) are included without village-level baseline infrastructure controls, and the household covariate vector X_i includes 2004 post-rollout variables (number of workers, owning a home business, receiving rental income) that are plausible downstream outcomes of land titling, risking post-treatment adjustment bias. A secondary propensity-score-matching trimming check only balances observed 2004 covariates across virtually completely overlapping support (Appendix Figure A1).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domain_ratings.justification: The 2004 Land Titling Special Project Survey sampled 3,204 rural households stratified across the coastal, highlands, and jungle regions and was specifically designed to represent both PETT program and non-program areas (Section 4(a), p. 5; Note 13, p. 12). However, because the survey was conducted in spring/summer 2004—up to 11 years after PETT phased-in implementation began in 1993—household inclusion in the rural sample occurred post-intervention. Since land titling lowers transaction costs for selling or renting land and alters household mobility (Section 2(a), pp. 2–3), differential compositional change in rural villages prior to 2004 cannot be ruled out, and sampling frame construction and household response rates are not detailed in the paper.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 5, Section 4(a); PDF Page 12, Note 13

domain_ratings.justification: In the modified DD estimator, exposure is defined by the interaction of village-level PETT arrival prior to the 2004 survey ('Program') and household lack of an alternative prior title ('No prior title'). While village-level PETT implementation is reasonably clear, pre-program household title status is not observed from pre-1993 cadastre records; instead, it is reconstructed retrospectively from 2004 self-reported title type under the assumption that all 'other titles' were held prior to PETT arrival (Note 19, p. 12). In non-program control villages that PETT had not yet reached by 2004, households could still have acquired non-PETT titles between 1993 and 2004, and retrospective self-reporting of legal title type is subject to recall or classification error.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domain_ratings.justification: The modified DD specification estimates an intention-to-treat policy effect of village-level PETT rollout among previously untitled rural households ('Program * NoPrior'), under which incomplete household take-up of PETT titles within program villages reflects real-world program delivery rather than protocol deviation. Section 3(b) (pp. 4–5) and Note 10 (p. 12) explicitly review concurrent Peruvian water-sector legislation, documenting that 1991–1996 privatization attempts were defeated and the 2004 IADB water reform loan occurred after the study period, reducing concern over confounding national water policy shifts.

domain_ratings.justification: Out of the 3,204 surveyed rural households reported in the summary statistics (Tables 1–3), 3,182 households (99.3%) are retained across all regression specifications in Tables 4, 5, 6, and 7, indicating very low item missingness (22 observations, or 0.7%). Although unit non-response in the underlying 2004 survey and exact missingness in the connection-date robustness check (Section 6(c)(i), p. 11) are not reported, missing data in the primary analytic sample is minimal.

domain_ratings.justification: All primary and secondary outcomes—household water supply source, composite 'improved water source', toilet/sanitation connection or septic system, electricity for lighting, realization of a public network connection within the prior 5 years, connection expenditure/financing, and perceived community service needs—are derived from unblinded household self-reports in the 2004 survey without utility records or physical verification. Notably, although Note 16 cites UNDP criteria for improved water (quality, <1 km proximity, >=20 L/day), the empirical 'improved water source' binary indicator simply codes any indoor tap, outdoor tap, fountain, or artisan well/spring as 1 (Table 3 Notes, p. 7) without verifying whether wells/springs are protected or safe. Five-year retrospective recall of connection timing and out-of-pocket costs (Table 6) is also susceptible to recall error.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of the reported result
domain_ratings.justification: There is no pre-registered protocol or pre-analysis plan, which is standard for retrospective econometric analyses of existing survey data but prevents verification against pre-specified outcome definitions and covariate sets. Furthermore, several empirical checks described in the text are omitted from the tables—specifically the secondary DD with propensity score matching ('we do not include separate results' tables for the DD with propensity score matching', p. 9) and regressions testing monthly water payment incidence and amounts ('results not shown', p. 11)—warranting Moderate concern.

overall_narrative_summary: Meeks (2018 [2017]) evaluates the impact of Peru's nationwide rural land-titling program (Special Rural Cadastre and Land Titling Project, PETT) on household water, sanitation, and electricity access using data on 3,204 rural households (analytic N = 3,182) from the 2004 Land Titling Special Project Survey. Employing a quasi-experimental modified difference-in-differences design (interacting village-level PETT arrival with household lack of prior property title, alongside region fixed effects and household covariates, plus an unreported propensity-score-matching common-support check), the paper finds statistically significant increases in access to improved water sources (+5.9 percentage points), sanitation/septic systems (+15.1 percentage points), and electricity (+8.8 percentage points), driven primarily by public/utility network connections within the preceding five years and complemented by out-of-pocket household investment only for sanitation. Appraised under ROBINS-I, the overall risk of bias is Serious, driven by Domain 1 (Confounding): because only a single 2004 post-rollout cross-section is available, pre-intervention parallel trends cannot be tested, village rollout timing may be endogenous, baseline village wealth/infrastructure is unmeasured beyond three broad regional fixed effects, and several regression controls (workers, home business, rental income) are post-treatment 2004 variables potentially affected by titling. Moderate risk of bias also arises in participant selection (post-rollout 2004 sampling without reported response rates), intervention classification (retrospective inference of pre-PETT 'other title' status from 2004 self-reports), outcome measurement (self-reported water/sanitation indicators without verifying spring/well protection or water quality), and selective reporting (no pre-analysis plan; unreported PSM-DD and monthly payment estimates), while missing data (0.7% in regressions) and deviations from intended interventions (checked against concurrent national water reforms) pose Low risk.
study_design_identified: Quasi-experimental non-randomized policy evaluation using a cross-sectional modified difference-in-differences design (exploiting spatial variation in phased-in village rollout of Peru's PETT land-titling program interacted with pre-program household title status, supplemented by difference-in-differences with propensity score matching) on a 2004 rural household survey (N = 3,204; analytic N = 3,182).

why_tool_chosen: The study evaluates the causal effect of a non-randomized government land-titling intervention (PETT) with explicit comparator groups (program vs. non-program villages interacted with prior-titled vs. previously untitled households) using a quasi-experimental modified difference-in-differences estimator and propensity score matching. Per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, ROBINS-I is the required appraisal tool for non-randomized quasi-experimental policy evaluations (DiD, PSM).
